title: Rama and Tataka
hookLine: Rama decides, and tries the gentlest way first
carry: ahimsa comes first, force only to protect

lines: MY FATHER TOLD ME TO OBEY YOU.
cards: Rama has listened, and his answer isn't a simple yes. My father told me to do whatever you say, he tells the sage. So I'll do this, for the sake of the cows, the sages and the land.
He's acting from obedience, from a promise, not from appetite for a fight. Then he lifts his bow and twangs the string. The sound rolls through the forest.
And from deep in the trees, something hears it and comes running.

teach.h: HE TRIES TO DISARM, NOT KILL.
teach.b: Tataka charges out, raising clouds of dust, hurling rocks. Valmiki slows down here. Rama doesn't try to kill her.
I'll just take away her power to harm, he tells Lakshmana; I don't want to take her life. He shoots and cuts off her arms. Lakshmana wounds her face.
That should end it. It doesn't.
Tataka uses her magic, turns invisible, changes shape, and rains stones on them from the air. Enough mercy, Rama, Vishvamitra calls. Evening is coming, and at dusk rakshasas grow stronger.
So Rama, tracking her by sound, looses an arrow, and Tataka falls. The gods praise Rama, Vishvamitra embraces him, and the forest, the text says, is freed and becomes beautiful again.
How do people read this scene? Traditional teachers see Rama's first act of protection, a land given back to its people, and point to how hard he tried not to kill.

Some modern readers find it painful, a young man pressed to kill a woman, and read it with that discomfort in view. Both readings take the text seriously. Underneath both is a tension Hinduism lives with honestly.

teach.h: AHIMSA, AND THE DUTY TO PROTECT.
teach.b: Ahimsa, not harming, is among its highest values. And a protector has a duty to stop those who are harming others.
The Ramayana shows the order Rama keeps. He asked first. He obeyed a promise.
He tried to disarm before he destroyed. Force came last, and only to protect.

how: In Ramayana recitation and performance, Tataka's defeat is told as Rama's first act of protecting the land; commentators and modern readers discuss it in different ways, and some draw attention to Rama's reluctance, reading it alongside ahimsa, the Hindu value of not harming.

o: a weapon Rama uses at dusk to end the fight
a forest spirit who guards the freed hermitages
the yakshi Rama first tried to disarm, not kill

games.q: the fight, in order — tap the pairs.
p: his father told him to obey the sage
not harming, a high Hindu value

s: Rama goes straight for the kill
he tells Lakshmana he only wants to take away her power to harm.
Vishvamitra warns that rakshasas grow stronger at dusk
so he tells Rama mercy has gone far enough.
in Hindu teaching, ahimsa means a protector may never use force
ahimsa is a high value, but a protector's dharma can call for force: last, and only to stop harm to others.

games.q: you're Rama. Tataka charges, hurling rocks. what's your first move, in the text?
games.why: he cuts off her arms, wanting only to take away her power to harm. only when her magic goes on does he loose the final arrow. ahimsa first, force last.

practice: Ahimsa starts small. Think of a situation where you have to be firm with someone, or will have to, and hold one question with the breath: what is the least harm that still protects the people who need protecting?
Don't plan the whole conversation; let the gentlest step that would actually work come into view, and rest with it. If you pray, ask for the strength to be both firm and kind.

wordCard.voice: Tataka. Rama, obeying his father's word, first tries to disarm her, and only when her magic goes on does he loose the arrow that frees the forest.

orig.note: Sanskrit tāṭakā: the yakshi of the forest. her defeat frees the land.

carryVoice: Your line: ahimsa comes first, force only to protect. Rama tried every gentler way first. That's day five hundred one.
